Why Ajay Shah gives his research ideas away freely

brief.head: Statement of purpose
brief.text: Springsteen wanted each record to be a statement of purpose, Amit Varma read, without being “damned by the term concept album”. {013-C03}

brief.head: Scarcity’s gift
brief.text: The old world’s scarcity created a few focal points of shared culture, Ajay Shah said: *Independence Day* means something to both hosts. {013-C13}

brief.head: Strangers’ eyes
brief.text: Growing up means moving beyond self-centredness, Ajay Shah said, riffing on a Roger Waters line. Springsteen’s songs of ordinary people showed him the beauty and magic in everyone’s lives. {013-C14}

brief.head: Copy it out by hand
brief.text: A student in Amit Varma’s writing course, whose first language is Hindi, copied Agota Kristof’s sentences out by hand to get the book’s rhythm into her head. {013-S14}

brief.head: The shortest highway
brief.text: Springsteen wrote that the E Street organist Danny Federici had “the shortest highway between his fingers and his heart”, Amit Varma recalled. {013-J19}

thought.text: I work to be an ancestor.
thought.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma: refusing to let his father’s ghosts have the last word

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Bruce Springsteen’s songs
lead.head: Rock and roll, by the book
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah timed this one to a birthday. Varma said the episode would come out on 22 September, the eve of Bruce Springsteen’s birthday, a date he has always known: his mother shares it.
When Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize for literature, many people were shocked, Varma said. He wrote an impassioned defence.
“To me, literature is words,” he said. “Literature is words, and below that, literature is storytelling.” Shakespeare, after all, wrote plays to be performed and read aloud. {013-C01}

Shah had two thoughts the moment Dylan won, he said: yes, that is literature; and Dylan before Springsteen? “It should have been the other way around.” That, he told listeners, is how two unlikely characters came to make this podcast.
## An eye-opener on a mini-CD
Shah’s account was personal. Seniors in his college hostel bought the LP of *Born in the USA* in 1984, but at the time he had ears only for Pink Floyd.
As a graduate student in America, he and Susan found a mini-CD with a live, acoustic *Born to Run*: “only Mr. Springsteen playing the mouth organ and a guitar and singing all by himself”. {013-S01}

It was an eye-opener. A three-CD live set followed, though Led Zeppelin had his ears then and Springsteen stayed a sideshow. Years later, at the Ministry of Finance in Delhi, the old albums started “coming to life” for him one by one.
## Four parts of a writer
Varma said he had no such coherent narrative. He offered four aspects of Springsteen’s work instead: the effort he made, the songs he wrote, the language he used and the change he embraced.

The effort came from the memoir, *Born to Run*: a rented guitar, an outplayed band, a song written in ten minutes. “Another way of thinking about it,” Varma said, “is that it took 30 years to write the song.” {013-C05}

The songs came from the people around him: his sister’s teenage marriage, his father’s paranoia, his blue-collar town. When writing students ask Varma what to write about, he tells them to look around them.
The language was plain. Springsteen never uses a word his listeners cannot understand, Varma said, yet he goes “a level deeper than you expect”. {013-C08}
He would never use a word like “polyglot”, Varma added, as Shah had at the start of the show. Springsteen knows what it means. He has just never used it.
And the change was constant. Springsteen refused to play “cover versions of himself”, and there are dozens of versions of *The River*.
## Ghosts and ancestors
The hosts ended where the memoir does some of its hardest work: with a father.

Springsteen wrote that in analysis “you work to turn the ghosts that haunt you into ancestors who accompany you”. Then: “I work to be an ancestor.” Varma saw a man aware of himself as a character in a longer story. {013-C12}
Shah turned one of their own lines around. Each of us is a linear combination of our influences; each of us is also adding to everyone else’s. So, he said, we should be the best version of ourselves.

Both closed on fathers and sons. Shah recommended *Independence Day*, Cat Stevens’s *Father and Son* and Cormac McCarthy’s *The Road*. Varma read A.K. Ramanujan’s *Self-Portrait*, about a face in a shop window “often signed in a corner by my father”.

second.label: The critic’s night
second.head: The future was on first
second.deck: Amit Varma on Jon Landau’s legendary review, and a partnership born of chance
body: On 9 May 1974, Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band opened for Bonnie Raitt. A young critic, Jon Landau, wrote a review that Amit Varma read out, including: “I saw rock and roll’s future, and his name is Bruce Springsteen.” {#future}

Landau was 27; Springsteen was 25. {#landauage} Springsteen, who never really had a father, saw him as one, and wrote that Landau was the first person he met “who had a language for discussing these ideas and the life of the mind”.
Ajay Shah was reminded of G. H. Hardy and Ramanujan: fascination with a genius, and care not to disrupt it. “I’m just so struck by this happenstance sort of connection,” Varma said. {013-S02}

quote.text: Both the passion of the fan and at the same time that ability to step back and note the craft

second.caption: Jon Landau’s legendary review

third.head: Cover star, empty pockets
body: In 1975 Bruce Springsteen was on the covers of *Time* and *Newsweek*. Then the tax authorities came knocking for back taxes. *Born to Run*, *Darkness on the Edge of Town* and *The River* were all huge successes, Amit Varma said, but until 1982 Springsteen did not make a single paisa. {#broke}

The lean years went back a long way. His early band, Steel Mill, found a club where nobody went and offered to play there, charging a dollar a head. Fifteen people came. The five members took $3 each. {#dollar}
Had *Born in the USA* flopped, Varma said, Springsteen would have been broke. “And that’s just a crazy thought.” {013-S13}
Ajay Shah drew a lesson for India, where everybody criticises the income tax authorities: “taxmen everywhere can be pretty cruel”.
third.caption: Springsteen’s years of back taxes

p2.title: Four sides of the Boss
p2.deck: How Ajay Shah found Springsteen, and Amit Varma’s case in four parts: effort, songs, language and change

sections.label: The listener
sections.head: Unplugged, then switched on
sections.caption: how he came to Springsteen
body: Ajay Shah came to Bruce Springsteen slowly, and the songs switched on in his mind one by one, years apart.

As a graduate student in America, he found a mini-CD of a 1988 show at the Los Angeles Coliseum, right next to his university. He had not gone. On it was an acoustic *Born to Run* that recast a song he had not liked on the album. {013-S01}
## A producer is an author

Shah drew on his own trade. If someone did for his research papers what a producer does for a band, he said, they would get authorship. George Martin for the Beatles and Brian Eno for U2 were “first-class participants in the creative journey”. {013-C02}

His own habit is to collect every live performance of one song and hear them in order. “No man can sing the same song twice,” he said. *Jungleland* in 1976 is brilliant; in 2012 a grown man tells a different story. {013-S11}

Long songs are a genre by themselves, Shah argued. *Stairway to Heaven* starts with an alaap and builds; *Jungleland* runs in reverse, from a wall of sound through what Springsteen calls the world’s greatest saxophone solo to the alaap at the end. {013-C04}

~ In Udaipur for a conference, lines from its close surfaced in his head: the poets around here “don’t write nothing at all. They just stand by and let it all be.” Between sessions, he played the song over and over.

quote.text: I learned in that period that a record producer is actually like a co-author.

sections.label: Aspect one: effort
sections.head: No natural genius, all graft
sections.caption: the work behind the genius
body: Rock stars seem to make it at 23, Amit Varma said; we don’t see that they have been at it since seven. The Beatles played hundreds and thousands of shows in Hamburg. Mozart was composing at five.

Springsteen, by his own account, was no natural genius. When Steel Mill was outplayed at a San Francisco audition, better talent did not scare him; what bothered him was “not maximizing my own abilities”. He went home knowing there would have to be changes. {013-S04}

Not everything was laboured. He wrote *Hungry Heart* in about ten minutes, and Bob Clearmountain mixed it in thirty seconds. Yet Springsteen wrote that they “could never have worked with Bob”, who was too fast; the E Street way was the hard way. {013-S07}
## A hundred Taj Mahals
Ajay Shah added a principle from chess and poker: volume. {#volume} Build not one Taj Mahal but a hundred, he said, because the others will fall by the wayside, and refinement comes from iteration.

Craft also compounds. In S. Chandrasekhar’s *Truth and Beauty*, Shah found Beethoven telling a friend, before the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music. He felt the same on first hearing *Devils and Dust*. {013-S12}
~ Varma’s moral for would-be artists was blunt: “boss, it takes work, it takes intentionality.”

quote.text: I had only one talent. I was not a natural genius. I would have to use every ounce of what was in me.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Aspect two: songs
sections.head: All in the family
sections.caption: a sister, a father and a town
body: Springsteen did not reach for myths or grand narratives, Amit Varma said. He turned to the people around him: his sister, his mother, his father and his small-town friends.

His father slid into paranoia, at one point believing love songs on the radio were a government ploy to get people married so they would pay more taxes. “I’m presuming there are greater taxes involved there,” Varma said. {013-J08}

In the memoir, a friendly boxing lesson in the living room turns when his father’s open-palm punches land a little too hard. The boy sees he is “an intruder, a stranger, a competitor in our home, and a fearful disappointment”. That relationship runs through *Independence Day*. {013-S09}
## Specific, so universal
“Most of my writing is emotionally autobiographical,” Springsteen wrote. That, Varma said, is why it reaches anyone: true to him, and true to everyone else. {013-C07}

*Darkness on the Edge of Town* is “just beautiful, simple language, and everyone relates”, he said. The method works even on a “non-metaphysical subject” like lust: in *I’m on Fire* the singer wakes with “a sheet soaking wet and a freight train running through the middle of my head”. {013-R18}
~ Varma also read Springsteen on the sixties: friends who were “real drug experimenting radicals”, and a construction-worker brother-in-law who “remained his whole life a man of the fifties”.

quote.text: I’ve learned you’ve got to pull up the things that mean something to you in order for them to mean anything to your audience.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Aspect three: words
sections.head: Plain speech, deep water
sections.caption: simple words that go deeper
body: Shakespeare was the box-office superstar of his day, Amit Varma said, because he wrote in the speaking rhythms of the day. Springsteen does the same: he never uses a word you can’t understand.

Simple is not shallow. *Secret Garden* seems carnal, then becomes a song about how you can never truly know another person. *Brilliant Disguise* asks whether a lover is wearing a mask, and ends by turning on the singer: “I damn sure don’t trust myself.” {013-C08}
Ajay Shah’s example was *Racing in the Street*, which begins as a song about cars and halfway through becomes “a psychological dive into the mind of a deeply sad person”. {#racing}
## Endings matter

Shah looks for a snap short sentence after a long one, “that power of four words, five words”. Varma pointed to Springsteen on children: “They are God giving you another shot.” It ends on a mute sound, he said. {013-C09}
Springsteen had found his voice by his late 20s. “What shit were we doing in our late 20s?” Varma asked. Shah: “We were writing really bad shit.” {013-J06}
~ Even Springsteen falters, Varma said. Of two sentences in a row in the memoir, the first “is crap”; the second “completely nails it”.

quote.text: Great poets know how you end a line matters.

sections.label: Aspect four: change
sections.head: Never his own tribute act
sections.caption: a career of constant change
body: Springsteen was determined not to be one of those musicians “always playing cover versions of himself”, Amit Varma said. As a boy, Varma heard a live *Growing Up* preceded by what seemed like half an hour of talk, and was entranced. {#growingup}
“Songs shift their meanings when you sing them,” Springsteen once said. There are 30, 40, 50 versions of *The River*, Varma said. {013-C10}

He nearly cut the piano from *Backstreets* before Jon Landau talked him out of it. Greil Marcus later heard in that opening music “so stately, so heartbreaking that it might be the prelude to a rock and roll version of the *Iliad*”. {#iliad}
## The right players

For his band, Springsteen wanted neither a one-man, one-vote democracy, “a ticking time bomb”, nor a nameless backing band. “You’re not looking for the best players,” he wrote. “You’re looking for the right players who click into something unique.”

Ajay Shah carried the idea to companies. Success corrodes equal partnerships, he said, as Simon and Garfunkel found; teams need shared values more than the world’s best drummer or technologist. {013-C11}
~ Shah recalled Paul McCartney supposedly saying Ringo Starr “was not even the best drummer in the Beatles”. Varma thought Paul too self-effacing for that.

quote.text: Songs shift their meanings when you sing them. They shift their meanings in time. They shift their meanings with who you sing them with.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: Amit Varma read from Bruce Springsteen’s autobiography, *Born to Run*, all through the episode. Of its passage on writing the title song, he said: “everyone should buy that book and read it to understand artistic process.” {#process}

contQuote.text: We each of us are adding to the linear combination of other people’s experiences. And I think that’s a great responsibility that we each of us should be the best version of ourselves because we are influencing so many people.

p3.title: Liner notes
p3.deck: Four stories behind the songs, and what each one teaches

stories.start: in his autobiography, he writes of a time where he was seven years old
stories.end: step by step by step we learn so much about the craft
stories.caption: a rented guitar
stories.kicker: From the memoir: a boy, a rented guitar and an audience
stories.head: The show before the chords
body: Bruce Springsteen was seven when he decided he had to have a guitar. He had heard something, or seen a photograph, and was struck. His mother could not afford to buy one, so she rented one.
For a few days the boy tried to play it. He simply could not figure it out.

Then came the sunny morning when it had to go back. He took it out to the backyard, where six or so of the neighbourhood kids were gathered, and gave what he called “my first and last show for quite a while”. {013-S03}

Amit Varma read the memoir’s account: “I held the guitar, I shook it, I shouted at it, I banged on it, I sang voodoo nonsense. I did everything but play it, all to their laughter and great amusement. I sucked.”
That afternoon he returned the guitar, “sad but a little relieved”. Yet for a moment in front of those kids, he wrote, he had smelled blood.
Later he got a guitar of his own, but did not know how to tune it. With the strings in whatever state they were in, he wrote a few tunes and played in front of the mirror, sure he was really cool.
Then someone tuned it for him, and taught him how. He realised that everything he had done before was rubbish.
~ For Varma, that is “such a great metaphor for how step by step by step we learn so much about the craft”. {#untuned}
stories.why: Mastery begins with incompetence plus desire. The boy could not play, but wanted it badly enough to put on a show anyway; the tuned guitar then showed him how much of the craft he had yet to learn.
stories.postscript: Max Weinberg, the E Street Band’s drummer, once said he had never seen anyone work as hard as Bruce Springsteen.

stories.start: And the first album is Greetings from Asbury Park, right?
stories.end: This gun's for higher. Even if it's just dancing in the dark
stories.caption: the hits written in a temper
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two demands for a hit, and the answers
stories.head: Want a hit? Have three
body: Bruce Springsteen turned in his debut, *Greetings from Asbury Park*, and Clive Davis handed it back: no hits, nothing for the radio. Springsteen went to the beach and wrote *Spirit in the Night*, then broke out his rhyming dictionary for *Blinded by the Light*.
Many artists, Amit Varma said, would insist on staying true to their art. “Springsteen doesn’t do that. He says, Fuck it, you want a hit, I’ll write you a hit.” {013-S06}

It happened again in 1984. *Born in the USA* was done when Jon Landau said they still needed a hit. {#landauhit} Furious, Springsteen went to his room and, as Varma imagined it, turned what he felt right then into *Dancing in the Dark*.
~ The tune is upbeat. The lyrics, Varma noted, are depressive: “I ain’t nothing but tired. Man, I’m just tired and bored with myself.”
stories.why: Constraint can be raw material. Where many artists treat a commercial demand as an insult to their art, Springsteen took it as a challenge, and his irritation became some of his best songs.

stories.start: So one little story. One fine day Bruce Springsteen wrote a song.
stories.end: rather than trying to protect oneself that, oh, this is my idea
stories.caption: the song Elvis never returned
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a song left on Elvis’s answering machine
stories.head: Elvis didn’t call back
body: One fine day Bruce Springsteen wrote a song called *Fire*, and heard in its lilt an Elvis Presley song. He got hold of Presley’s number and called. The call went to an answering machine, so Springsteen sang the song into it and dictated the lyrics.
Presley ignored him. Springsteen gave the song to the Pointer Sisters, who made it a number-one hit; his own later live versions are, to Ajay Shah, the best.

Shah took a rule for life from it. “I learned one thing, which is just gift your stuff away,” he said. “Don’t try to hold everything, don’t try to hang on to everything.” {013-S10} All his life, he has given research ideas away freely.
~ Shah had paused mid-story for the young: “Oh, ye young reader, please go Google what is an answering machine.” {013-J07}

quote.text: It’s better to keep on inventing and giving things away rather than trying to protect oneself that, oh, this is my idea.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s footnote: The Replacements once asked, “How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?” {013-R26}

stories.start: For example, he writes about his sister in the book.
stories.end: which all of us experience. And there's such magic in it.
stories.caption: his sister’s shotgun wedding
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a family drama that became a song
stories.head: Union card and wedding coat
body: Bruce Springsteen’s sister Virginia became pregnant at 17, dropped out of high school and married the father, Mickey Shave. In Springsteen’s telling, Mickey was an arrogant, leather-jacketed, bull-riding greaser from Lakewood, and eventually an all-round great guy.
Virginia, who “had never boiled water, washed a dish, or swept a floor”, became a hardcore Irish working woman. Mickey worked in construction.
“Which song did this inspire?” Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah got there first: “I got a job working in construction.”
It was *The River*, in which Mary is seventeen and the narrator, for his 19th birthday, gets “a union card and a wedding coat”. {#mary}
~ Springsteen needed no myths. “His sister gets pregnant and gets married, he writes about that,” Varma said. {013-S08}
stories.why: Ordinary family drama was enough. When his writing students ask what to write about, Varma tells them to look around them: Springsteen’s sister, his father and his town were all the material he needed.

quiz.q: Which critic wrote, after a Bonnie Raitt show, that he had seen rock and roll’s future?
quiz.a: Jon Landau, who later became Springsteen’s producer and a father figure to him.

quiz.q: Whom did Springsteen pitch *Fire* to, and who finally turned it into a hit?
quiz.a: Elvis Presley, via an answering machine; the Pointer Sisters took it to number one.

quiz.q: How long did Springsteen take to write *Hungry Heart*, and Bob Clearmountain to mix it?
quiz.a: About ten minutes to write it, and thirty seconds to mix it.

quiz.q: What did Springsteen’s father believe the love songs on the radio were really for?
quiz.a: A government ploy to get people married so that they would pay more taxes.

quiz.q: How, by Ajay Shah’s account, does *Jungleland* reverse the shape of *Stairway to Heaven*?
quiz.a: It opens with a wall of sound and ends on the alaap.

quiz.q: What did a student in Amit Varma’s writing course do with Agota Kristof’s novels?
quiz.a: She copied the sentences out by hand to get their rhythm into her head.
